item.title: Can You Still Work in Testing Without Coding Skills
item.description:
Many people from non-IT backgrounds who want to switch to testing have heard it said that software testing has a low barrier to entry—that you can get into the industry even without knowing how to code. So is that actually the case?

The answer should be stated plainly:

Without coding skills, you actually can work in software testing—and yet, in practice, you actually cannot.

Why you actually can

Software testing is not a discipline built on coding ability, which is why, in principle, you can do it.

Software testing is the act of exposing quality problems in a product through testing; it is, in essence, a skill of discovering the unknown. What matters more, then, are abilities such as experimentation, exploration, observation, reasoning, questioning, and modeling. Having coding skills, on the other hand, mostly helps you understand how the product is implemented, or lets you use code to extend your testing methods and improve testing efficiency. In this sense, coding ability is a supporting capability—one that assists the testing work, but is by no means the decisive factor in whether that work can be accomplished!

In his paper “Testing and Checking”, James Bach elaborated on the relationship between testing and checking

testing is the broader concept, while checking is only a subset of testing—and checking itself is further divided into manual checking and checking performed with the help of machines (tools).

What coding ability affects, then, falls mostly within that tool-assisted checking part.

That is why, in the early days, many testing experts who excelled at the work were not particularly good at coding; more often than not, they were domain experts in the relevant business area, equipped with outstanding testing thinking—that is, the detective-like abilities of observation and reasoning mentioned above.

So, in truth, lacking coding skills does not prevent you from doing testing work exceptionally well.

Why you actually cannot

And yet, we must also say that, without coding skills, in practice you really cannot.

As we noted above, in the early days there were indeed testing experts who could not code. But times have changed, and the reality today is quite different. As the industry has evolved, the direction of the testing profession has arguably departed from its original track. It is rather lamentable, and worthy of a sigh!

There are several reasons:

The rise of development models that emphasize fast delivery, such as Agile

In Agile development models, there is in fact no longer a dedicated testing role; instead, the emphasis is on team members being versatile generalists who can take on a range of development tasks with one specialty and many skills—including both development and testing. As a member of the team, a tester naturally cannot do testing alone; when necessary, they must also be able to pick up development work, at least including tasks originally in the developer’s domain such as unit testing and integration testing. Coding ability is, of course, the hard requirement for meeting this condition.

The mandatory requirement for test automation skills

Also driven by the needs of development models such as Agile and continuous integration, test automation has become an indispensable part of the process. And as the foundational capability for test automation, coding ability is naturally a necessity.

But it must be pointed out here that something like test automation—aimed at “quickly completing testing”—is, according to the relationship between testing and checking shown in the figure above, not really “testing” at all; it is much more “checking”. A single-minded emphasis on coding ability is, in a sense, actually a weakening of the requirements of testing work—that is, it increasingly demands only “checking” rather than “testing”.

The talent market is oversupplied

Finally, there is the industry environment. In the early days of the internet boom, the talent gap was large, and a great deal of “verification” work was done manually by junior staff or complete beginners with zero foundation who did not need coding skills; manual “checking” accounted for a larger share.

But when the industry turns downward, companies cut costs, leading to an oversupplied talent market. The entry barrier naturally rises, job requirements climb accordingly, and expectations for tool-based “verification” grow higher—so coding ability, test automation, tool development, and the like have all but become must-have skills.

Layered on top of that is the current prevalence of development models such as Agile and the resulting demand for test automation. It is fair to say that, without coding skills, in today’s environment it has become very hard to argue that one can still work in testing—there is simply no way in.

Conclusion

So, under present conditions, when it comes to testing work, lacking coding skills does not mean you cannot accomplish the work—but without coding ability it has become very difficult to get on board.

Therefore, as individuals swept along by the tide of the times, what we can do is not to swim against the current, but to steadily build personal capabilities that move with the trend. But we must still understand what the core requirements of this work truly are—accumulate steadily and then burst forth, for gold only appears after all the sand is washed away!

item.title: Is Agile a Panacea for Most Projects? Some Reflections on Agile
item.description:
In modern project management, agile development is becoming increasingly popular; agile is invoked at every turn, as if not being agile means falling behind the times. Is agile really a panacea for modern software projects? Is it truly a universally applicable development method?

The Origins of Agile

Let me start with the conclusion: agile development is in fact a method with considerable limitations, and it is not universally applicable! It grew and thrived simply because it aligned with the rapid growth of the Internet and matched the needs of Internet applications for changing requirements and frequent releases fairly well.

Compared with traditional software, Internet software also features incremental delivery, the ability to fix online issues quickly, and a relatively higher tolerance for quality problems. All this makes agile development easier to land in Internet projects.

And as Internet giants adopted agile methods and agile institutions promoted them vigorously, today agile seems to have become a universal method that applies everywhere. Various frameworks for applying agile have also emerged, such as Scrum, SAFe, LeSS, Nexus, and so on.

But when we look at how these frameworks developed and the scenarios where they are applied, we find that each framework carries considerable constraints. Small frameworks such as Scrum impose specific limits on team size and require meeting ceremonies; large frameworks such as SAFe impose requirements on organizational structure, multiple supporting roles, and dedicated teams. And so on…

The birth of large frameworks, too, came about through evolution in response to the real operation of actual projects; they were meant to address problems in specific scenarios, with more roles, ceremonies, and processes continuously added like bricks and tiles. Yet this seems to be retracing the development trajectory of traditional software R&D processes, and likewise racing headlong toward high-complexity teams!

The Limitations of Agile

So we cannot help but reflect: is agile really a method with universal applicability? Is it a panacea for solving traditional problems?

We cannot deny the positive value of the ideas agile emphasizes, such as collaboration and responding to change; the Agile Manifesto itself was an extremely necessary reform of rigid, traditional software processes.

The problem, however, is that agile was born out of reflection on software development processes. Without exception, the seventeen experts who proposed the Agile Manifesto all came from the field of software development. We cannot say that these masters’ thinking and vision were not ahead of their time, but the Manifesto itself was mainly a set of solutions proposed for the original problems in the domain of software development.

In other words, agile methods are inherently aimed only at software development, not at software products and project management. To form a software project and run a product, besides development there are other roles such as product, design, operations, customer service, quality, and security. The absence of these roles means that when the method is applied at the product level, it lacks targeted thinking from the corresponding perspectives, and instead focuses mostly on the problems that the development role encounters within the product.

Precisely because of this inherent limitation, agile tends to run into all kinds of problems in real-world application. During a project’s incubation period, when the focus is on R&D, agile is at its most valuable. But once a product gets on track and needs to coordinate with more different units and roles, agile often starts to show that it is not up to the task.

The Value of Agile

The success of any enterprise or project, in fact, cannot be separated from two things, systems and culture.

  • Agile methods, because of their inherent limitations, are not universally applicable as a system.
  • But the culture and values conveyed by agile methods are where the value of agile truly lies. Whether or not you adopt agile methods, even if you use traditional processes, embracing agile values can still help a project succeed.

Just my humble opinion. For more introductory articles on agile development, please refer to the collection.

item.title: Why Did DeepSeek Choose Open Source?
item.description:
Someone asked: the major large models abroad are basically all closed source, so why did DeepSeek, being so capable, choose to open source?

To answer this question, you actually only need to understand who Liang Wenfeng is, how he made his start, and a few of his interviews available online, and it becomes clear!

DeepSeek Is a Product of Interest

As one of China’s leading quantitative private funds, High-Flying has dominated the field by relying on AI technologies such as machine learning, and it has already been enormously successful. In other words, High-Flying already earns more than enough money on its own; building the DeepSeek large model on top of its existing technical accumulation is more a product of the founders’ personal interest than a core product. At most, the original intent was to empower its core business—but it was absolutely never its main track.

Of course, now that DeepSeek has reached this position, it is not out of the question that High-Flying’s direction could become large models in the future.

It is just like Nokia originally making pulp, or Lamborghini originally making tractors…. An unintentional result that took root.

So the first consideration in building DeepSeek was not the business model, not how to make money! Whether to open source or stay closed source was not much of a dilemma in terms of business model!

The Core of Technology Is Not the Technology Itself, but the Talent That Produces It

And from Liang Wenfeng’s interviews, we can also learn his view on open source: people are the key to innovation! In the face of a disruptive innovation like AI, the moat gained through closed source is extremely short-lived; it is passionate, curious, daring top talent that is the source of such technology!

He also gave the example of NVIDIA: there is nothing particularly secret about NVIDIA’s technology itself, but assembling a team, building an ecosystem, and catching up all take time—and that time is the real moat!

The confidence in one’s bones and the sense of mission to take the world upon oneself

In his interviews, Liang Wenfeng repeatedly spoke about how China’s earlier technological development was mostly that of a follower, with incremental, fine-tuning innovations but a lack of disruptive innovation. There is a need to move from the imitation stage toward original creation, and to reflect Chinese contributions within the progress of human technology. I believe this is also the result of his giving the all-domestic talent on his team, on the foundation of his financial strength, ample freedom and room to innovate, accumulating strength over time and then breaking through!

Liang Wenfeng has truly lived up to the ideal: when you succeed, help the whole world succeed

item.title: How to Complete Testing Quickly
item.description:
A reader asked how to complete testing quickly when the team has no dedicated testers.

Let me start with the conclusion: there is no standard answer here!

Having no testing role only means there is no one specifically responsible for this function; but the work of testing itself has not disappeared.

“Completing testing quickly” is really better put as “quickly building quality confidence.”

Because testing is endless, there is no such thing as absolutely “finishing testing.” Based on past experience or a general consensus, once everyone basically agrees the product is probably fine, testing counts as done.

So if what we want is to quickly build this quality confidence — or to quickly reach a consensus with stakeholders that quality is OK — what factors should we consider along these lines?

Scope to Be Tested

One way to finish testing quickly is to have a small test scope — for example, a tiny change with no related affected modules, so a quick check is enough. The logic is the same as committing development code promptly and integrating frequently: don’t accumulate changes, so you save the time of tracing back through a pile of changes when something goes wrong.

Do thorough self-testing during development and integrate and test in time; don’t accumulate changes.

Existing Quality

Another aspect is whether you have confidence in the product’s existing quality. Development is incremental, so was the quality of the existing baseline up to standard? Are the relationships and impacts between the new and existing parts all known? Product quality is holistic; historical features and their effects also bear on current quality confidence. So whether the relationship between new and existing parts is clear, and whether the existing baseline itself is sound, are also critical.

Potential Problems

Then again, testing is black-box, so you can’t clearly know how much danger lies beneath the iceberg. But quality confidence actually has no direct relationship with potential problems; it mainly relates to known problems and tested scope — the fewer known problems and the larger the tested scope, the stronger the confidence. The logic behind it: more known problems often mean more potential ones; spotting one cockroach may mean a whole nest of them. So the emphasis is still on the quality of what’s handed over for testing! If self-testing isn’t thorough, don’t move on to integration testing yet — every developer should first sweep their own little patch clean.

Risk of Problems Surfacing

Finally, there is one more firewall: the risk of problems surfacing. A problem surfaces — boom! But the impact of that “boom” varies: is it just a spark that dies out, or does it blow a hole, or even bring down the whole building? Beyond the size of the problem itself, different products have different tolerance for problems. Setting off a firecracker in a building slated for demolition just means it gets demolished a bit early — tolerance is high, so confidence is high!

Summary

Taking all of the above together, completing testing quickly ultimately comes down to whether you can build delivery confidence as soon as possible, which depends on individual capability, product characteristics, and the development process. It’s really a matter of mindset.

Lastly, it has to be said: nothing can defy its inherent laws. A system that runs stably, is robust and hard-wearing can only be achieved through all kinds of running-in and tempered by all kinds of internal and external problems.

The “fast delivery” and “winning it all in one battle” you imagine — there is no such thing as peaceful times; it’s just that someone else is carrying the weight for you. And the one carrying it might be the developers in the early stage, the testers, or the operations staff — or, in the end, the users who bear it all!

item.title: Musk's Audit Storm, an AI Shock More Direct Than DeepSeek
item.description:
During the Spring Festival holiday, everyone here was celebrating in high spirits. The box office of Ne Zha kept climbing; DeepSeek also broke into the mainstream, dominating everyone’s feeds, with its servers busy for long stretches.

At the same time, across the ocean, as Trump moved into the White House on January 20, Musk also took charge of DOGE and got to work at lightning speed that very day, launching a large-scale audit of federal government spending.

This DOGE is not the cryptocurrency DOGE; it is short for the U.S. Department of Government Efficiency.

Musk and the DOGE Audit Storm

Unlike the traditional large-scale audits we might imagine — first setting up an audit department, then hundreds or even thousands of auditors spending months on preparation, on-site work, and reconciliation — DOGE has, in less than 20 days, already turned American politics upside down.

— January 20: shut down the Chief Diversity Officers Executive Council (CDOEC);

— January 25: canceled about $420 million in existing / soon-to-be-signed contracts;

— January 27: the Departments of Labor, Transportation, Agriculture, Commerce, Health and Human Services, and the Treasury canceled 16 DEIA contracts, saving $145 million;

— January 28: the General Services Administration (GSA) terminated three leases on nearly empty office space and shut down 17 DEIA websites, saving $1.6 million;

— January 29: canceled a $45 million DEI scholarship for Myanmar;

(As of January 29, 2025, 26 departments including the Department of Education and the GSA had terminated 85 DEIA-related contracts totaling about $1 billion;)

— February 3: the number of terminated leases on underutilized buildings rose to 22, and the savings grew from $1.6 million to $44.6 million;

— February 3: shut down the United States Agency for International Development (USAID);

— February 4: six agencies terminated 36 contracts, saving about $165 million in total, including the Department of Homeland Security’s “Humanities Research and Climate Support Services” contract;

— February 5: terminated 12 consulting contracts (at the GSA and the Department of Education), saving about $30 million in total;

— February 6: the Social Security Administration terminated its “Gender X Initiative Marker” contract, saving over $1 million; NASA canceled its Politico subscription, saving $500,000; 78 contracts in the DEI, distressed assets, media, and consulting categories were terminated, for total savings of about $110 million;

— February 8: announced that within the past 48 hours, the Department of Health and Human Services had canceled 62 contracts worth $182 million; the Department of Education terminated three DEI training grants totaling $15 million.

Yet behind such fast and efficient audit results and actions there is no massive team — it relies on nothing more than a few geniuses barely in their twenties, backed by their AI algorithms.

DOGE’s Six Young Prodigies

Hard to imagine, but every move on the list above was carried out by the six young men below.

  • Gavin Kliger (25): A graduate of UC Berkeley in electrical engineering and computer science, Kliger was formerly a senior software engineer at the U.S. AI data analytics company Databricks and is an expert in artificial intelligence and big data analysis. His job is to draft executive orders and ensure they take effect quickly within the government — the email telling all USAID staff they need not return to headquarters on Monday came from his hand. He also directly drafted the funding review order targeting the U.S. Treasury, took part in OPM’s mass layoff plan, and was responsible for setting the “rehire standards” for civil servants, requiring that future government employees be approved by DOGE before being hired.

  • Luke Farritor (23): Farritor dropped out of the University of Nebraska–Lincoln and later worked for Nat Friedman, the Silicon Valley entrepreneur behind GitHub. He once interned at SpaceX, writing software for the pumps, valves, and other components that help fuel rockets. Farritor is currently listed as an “executive engineer” in the office of the Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS), and personally oversaw the digital lockdown operation at USAID; his next target is already the systems of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, which handles contracts.

  • Edward Coristine (19): The youngest of the group, Coristine had just graduated from high school and was studying mechanical engineering and physics at Northeastern University in Boston. He spent three months last summer working at Musk’s brain-computer interface company Neuralink, and his specific duties have not yet been made clear. Coristine once joined a call with U.S. General Services Administration employees using a non-government Google Gmail account, asking them to review code he had written and justify their own work — a move that sparked dissatisfaction among federal employees.

  • Akash Bobba (21): Bobba comes from UC Berkeley and was an investment engineering intern at Bridgewater Associates; he had also interned at Meta and at Palantir, the U.S. software services company founded by MAGA backer Peter Thiel. He specializes in artificial intelligence, data analysis, and financial modeling. He is responsible for designing algorithms to monitor the flow of government funds, leading a “real-time fiscal spending monitoring system” that allows federal “inefficient spending” to be frozen in real time without congressional review.

  • Ethan Shaotran (22): A senior computer science major at Harvard, Shaotran is the only one on the team with AI startup experience. The AI company he founded, Energize AI, received $100,000 in funding from OpenAI, and he once took second place in a hackathon held by Musk’s AI company xAI. Shaotran leads DOGE’s AI government initiative, whose goal is to replace the government’s traditional human decision-making with algorithms, automating most administrative approvals, budget evaluations, and even congressional reports.

  • Gautier Cole Killian (24): Breached the Treasury’s security systems and obtained access to the payment network. A graduate of McGill University, Killian is exceptionally strong in financial data processing and once worked as an engineer at Jump Trading, a firm specializing in high-frequency financial trading and algorithms. His main task is to help the DOGE team break through the Treasury’s security defenses, giving them access to the government payment network and letting them bypass security checks to read millions of transaction records directly. Killian is also one of the few young people granted senior White House access, and Musk places extremely high trust in him.

So these few engineers, barely out of college, after obtaining data access and in only about two weeks, used AI to bring to the surface all sorts of problems that had lain hidden beneath the iceberg for decades. You could say it truly was a case of speed being everything — the bureaucrats over in the U.S. probably hadn’t even come to their senses before finding their house had been raided.

Reflections

No matter where this reform storm ultimately takes Musk and his six young lieutenants, AI has already, in a jaw-dropping way, begun to sway the political situation across the ocean, and it is bound to deeply affect every aspect of our lives.

item.title: Scrum's Four Ceremonies: The Sprint Retrospective
item.description:
In the earlier articles, we have already gone over the key points of holding the planning meeting, the daily standup, and the review meeting. In this article, we take a look at the last meeting ceremony among Scrum’s four major Agile ceremonies — the Sprint Retrospective.

The Purpose and Role of the Retrospective

Because the retrospective and the review meeting are both usually placed on the last day of the iteration and are typically scheduled back to back, many people mistakenly think the two meetings are the same Agile ceremony and treat them as one and the same.

This is in fact a misunderstanding of two distinct ceremonies — the review and the retrospective. The two meetings differ markedly in their function, purpose, and even participants, so one should not assume they are the same meeting simply because the two ceremonies are consecutive in time.

The review meeting’s main purpose is, through a demonstration of the iteration’s deliverables, to collect feedback and opinions from product stakeholders in time, so as to confirm that the phased delivery meets expectations and to make timely adjustments to subsequent iterations. Its focus is externally oriented feedback collection, aimed at the product itself.

The retrospective’s focus, by contrast, is on internal team review and summary, aimed at process and team collaboration.

So the purpose of the retrospective is, after an iteration ends, to look back and inspect how the iteration ran, drawing out experience and lessons from it.

Holding a retrospective produces the following benefits:

  • While working across multiple iterations toward the product vision, the team also regularly inspects how the iterations run, discovering problems, summarizing experience, improving in time, and steadily getting better.
  • Through the retrospective as a window, team members have a relatively formal and open platform where anyone can raise suggestions about how the team works or point out possible problems.
  • The retrospective is also an important ceremony for strengthening team cohesion, and a channel for team members to affirm one another or exchange views frankly and openly.

In short, the retrospective can be seen as a closed-door meeting within the team, a ceremony of the team’s self-renewal and self-optimization.

The Different Roles in the Retrospective

So, given the purpose above, this meeting should not be held as the same meeting as the review meeting either.

The roles that different people play in the meeting also differ:

  • Must attend: As an internal team summary meeting aimed at the team’s own improvement, the Dev Team and Scrum Master must take part.

  • Attend if possible: Although the PO is also part of the team, the PO’s responsibilities are oriented more toward the product itself, and they are basically not directly involved in product development. So when it comes to the team retrospective, the PO is not required to attend; but as an important member of the team, in many cases some opinions and improvement actions do need to be raised or joined by the PO, so the PO attends whenever possible.

  • Avoid attending: One important reason for separating the retrospective from the review meeting is precisely that, as an internal improvement meeting, some stakeholders who attend the review meeting — such as users and management — had best avoid attending, so that team members can express their views more directly. Of course, in certain special circumstances, such as major disagreements or serious risks to product goals, key stakeholders may also be invited to the retrospective. (And of course, if the boss insists on attending, it is generally hard to refuse.)

Meeting Process

The retrospective is generally recommended to be held in person as much as possible. And because the team members all know one another well and the iteration has just ended, the atmosphere should be made as relaxed as possible; preparing some small snacks and little gifts helps the meeting achieve a better effect.

The general flow of the meeting is as follows:

  1. First of all, of course, the Scrum Master facilitates the meeting. Before the retrospective begins, some preparation is usually needed. For example, collect relevant data from the iteration, such as the burn-down chart and the team’s velocity chart, as well as the current status of follow-up items from previous iterations’ retrospectives; all of this is reviewed by the team as a whole at the start of the meeting. And for relatively new teams, the rules of the retrospective also need to be explained, along with the supporting tools to be used, such as cards and voting stickers.

  2. The next segment is to collect the team’s suggestions about how the iteration ran. That is, each team member writes down their own observations of the current iteration — which aspects went well and should be kept, which aspects were not good enough and could be improved, including anyone they would like to thank individually — on stickers of different colors. Once everyone has finished writing, the stickers are placed in the corresponding areas of a prepared whiteboard. After the opinions are collected, everyone gathers in front of the whiteboard, and the SM or any member of the team reads aloud the content of each sticker card. This process is effectively the team reliving together how the iteration ran.

  3. After all the opinions have been read out, the meeting moves into the voting segment. For example, everyone may be given 3 votes, and then, among these opinions, each person votes for the 3 they think most worth taking action on in the next iteration.

  4. Once voting is done, tally the opinions with the most votes. For example, with three votes per person, the three opinions with the most votes are finally selected as the to-do items to take action on in the next iteration.

  5. After the to-do items are set, the team also jointly discusses the concrete measures for each item and decides how to carry out the improvement and enhancement.

  6. The results produced by the discussion above must be made concrete down to implementable actions, with a designated owner for each. These are to be arranged as tasks for the next iteration and added to the iteration board for task tracking.

Through the meeting process above, the goal of the team’s continuous self-renewal and improvement is achieved. A very important core here is that members should be frank and open, and that everyone truly conducts the retrospective from the starting point of improving the team itself.

Common Retrospective Tools

The main content of a retrospective is, in fact, collecting everyone’s observations of how the iteration ran and their suggested improvements. In an in-person setting this is usually represented on a whiteboard using stickers of different colors.

But nowadays many teams may be working in different locations or from home; for such online retrospectives, some online supporting tools can also be used.

The more commonly used ones include:

IdeaBoardZ

A retrospective template can be conveniently created through https://ideaboardz.com/.

Following the most basic

  • Things the team did well
  • Things worth improving
  • Actions to be taken

Collect everyone’s opinions from these aspects

Starfish

Besides the basic model above, some teams also use the Starfish to break down the observations into five different areas.

  • KEEP: Behaviors that should be kept going
  • MORE: Behaviors that should be done more
  • LESS: Behaviors that should be reduced in later iterations
  • START: Behaviors that should be started in later iterations
  • STOP: Behaviors that should be stopped in later iterations

Sailboat

Similarly, there are also models like the Sailboat, whose purpose is basically the same — all serving the goal of reviewing and inspecting, and learning from past experience for the future.

Summary

The above is a rundown of the Sprint Retrospective. In actual practice, never let the retrospective turn into a session of complaining, griping, or mutual blame. No matter how serious the problems discovered during the process are, everyone should ultimately stay grounded in the team’s development — the real purpose is for both the members and the team to improve together.

item.title: A Closer Look at Agile: The Sprint Review
item.description:
In the previous two articles, we shared the planning meeting and the daily standup among the four Agile ceremonies. In this article, we continue by introducing the Agile Sprint Review meeting, held after an Agile Sprint ends.

Purpose and Role

As a meeting held at the end of a Sprint iteration, the Sprint Review Meeting mainly embodies the Agile ideas of “customer collaboration” and “fast feedback,” and is an important expression of the Agile principle of moving in small, fast steps.

To be specific, the purpose of this meeting is to demonstrate the current Sprint’s work results to the product’s business team, users, and stakeholders, to hear their feedback on the product, and to confirm whether the current product output — the Increment — meets expectations and whether there are new opinions, so that later Sprints can be adjusted in time.

This is also a notable difference between Agile and traditional development models: within a short Sprint cycle, progress is confirmed in time with the ultimate requester through the demonstration at this meeting, rather than — as in traditional processes — waiting until a long, complete development cycle has passed before delivering the final product to users for confirmation.

So, beyond the team’s delivery of results, the more important role of this meeting is to obtain feedback from external business parties and other stakeholders through the demonstration of the product Increment, so as to allow timely adjustment.

Misconceptions

Many people regard this meeting as a delivery-confirmation meeting held inside the Sprint team with the PO, but that is actually incorrect.

It is based more on the purpose of communicating with parties outside the team.

For the same reason, under some special circumstances this meeting may be skipped for certain Sprints. For example:

  • When the Sprint’s Increment produces no obvious, directly demonstrable business change, and consists more of technical adjustments or architecture-level changes, there is little that needs confirmation from the business side.

  • When key business parties or stakeholders cannot attend and cannot match the current Sprint’s cadence. A Sprint’s end time is fairly fixed, but if key stakeholders’ schedules cannot align, the meeting may be cancelled. In that case, a later Sprint’s review meeting will include a demonstration of the current sprint’s relevant output.

  • When the team itself assesses that the Sprint Goal was not achieved and the key output falls short of expectations, it is naturally not suitable to give a product demonstration to external parties.

Attendees

Given this meeting’s purpose, a review meeting may in fact involve quite a lot of people, generally including the following roles:

  • The Scrum Team should of course all attend, including the PO, SM, and Dev Team.
  • Key stakeholders, usually the product’s sponsors (roles such as the product director / R&D director).
  • The reporting lines of team members — development manager, testing manager, UE manager, and so on.
  • Other key roles from teams associated with the Sprint’s output, such as key members of other collaborating Scrum teams (PO, SM), or functions like security, legal, quality, after-sales, pre-sales, and customer service.

The review meeting is generally held on the last day of the Sprint. Within the Scrum Team, the PO — as the communication channel with the various external stakeholders — sends out the meeting invitation before the meeting (usually 1–2 days in advance). This both informs the relevant people of the current Sprint’s main input content and scope, and helps confirm the attendees, while leaving the team some necessary preparation time for the review demonstration.

Meeting Process

On the last day of the iteration, everyone finishes the iteration work and, following the PO’s meeting invitation, takes part in the Review Meeting.

The meeting process is roughly as follows:

  1. The Scrum Master facilitates the meeting. Usually at the start they welcome the attending stakeholders and briefly introduce the participants. If a new member has joined the Scrum Team, they may also ask the new member to give a brief self-introduction. If everyone is already familiar with one another, it is just a short opening remark.

  2. Next, the PO explains the main content of the current Sprint increment, which is also the main functional scope to be demonstrated. If the Review is held only after several sprints have passed, this part usually covers the content of multiple Sprints.

  3. Then comes the demonstration segment. Generally the PO gives the demonstration and explanation themselves, because the PO is involved in the Sprint throughout and is fairly familiar with the relevant content. In practice, a team member who knows the relevant features well can also give the demonstration, and it is often the people responsible for testing who perform it. It is best not to switch frequently between different people during the demonstration.

  4. The following segment usually runs throughout the demonstration as well: feedback and communication from stakeholders on the product implementation. Based on the product’s goals and value, and including expectations for the next Sprint, they may have questions or suggestions for improvement about the product, and the team can communicate and discuss these issues directly with the stakeholders. This part actually takes up the largest share of the meeting’s time; the atmosphere may be harmonious or heated, but in the end it leads to some revisions or additions to the original requirements.

  5. So the output of the previous segment actually produces an updated PBI list, which will also be the main input for subsequent Sprints and the material the PO needs to further organize and refine after the meeting.

  6. Finally, the SM summarizes the meeting, usually recapping the discussion results, including confirming the requirements and other matters to be tracked and implemented afterwards, such as research and tackling of related technologies. Of course, this summary also serves to signal to stakeholders that the meeting is over, but for the team it is also a reminder that the retrospective will follow (the retrospective is usually held right after the review meeting).

The review meeting is generally kept within two hours (for a two-week Sprint). During the meeting the SM must control the pace and, depending on how much is being demonstrated, keep discussions that become too divergent or too deep within the time budget — for example by scheduling a separate dedicated meeting to discuss them.

Summary

So, to summarize the key points of the review meeting:

  1. First, this is a meeting held after an iteration ends to obtain feedback on the iteration’s output. It is a major expression of the Agile idea of moving in small, fast steps. But in actual practice, it is not a meeting that must be held every single Sprint. The only requirement is to avoid leaving the gap too long, so that the team retains the flexibility to make timely adjustments based on stakeholder feedback.

  2. This meeting is not an acceptance meeting; it is not used to confirm with the PO whether the Sprint Goal was achieved. Communication and feedback are the main purposes.

  3. The meeting’s process and output are an important part of Agile iteration and product evolution, and an important process for determining PBIs and correcting course in time, ensuring that the team’s work matches users’ expectations.

  4. Finally, this meeting is also the only formal window in the Sprint for the Dev Team to communicate directly with relevant stakeholders, to feel the pressure, and to face the real thoughts of users or bosses. It is of great significance for preventing the team from working in isolation, taking things for granted, or slipping into an engineer-only mindset.

The above is a rundown and summary of the key points for holding the Sprint Review Meeting. Feel free to follow Qiucao for more in-depth reviews and reflections on software development, testing, and technology.

item.title: A Closer Look at Agile: The Daily Standup
item.description:
In the previous article, we discussed the key points of running Sprint Planning, one of the four Agile ceremonies. In this article, we continue with the second of the four ceremonies — the one held most frequently, the one teams find easiest to adopt, and yet the one most likely to go off the rails: the Daily Standup.

Misconceptions about the Daily Standup

The standup is a fairly emblematic ceremony. Most teams that claim to be Agile also adopt this practice, yet when it comes to understanding the standup, there are in fact quite a few misconceptions.

  1. Many people assume the standup is a meeting owned by the Scrum Master. They understand it as a meeting like those in a traditional project, where the PM listens to the team report on their work.

But in Scrum, the SM is actually a supporting role; the team itself is the one accountable for all the concrete work. So the real Owner of the standup is the team. Although the SM usually facilitates it, the SM’s main function is to coordinate and keep the pace, while the meeting itself exists primarily to enable the team’s own internal collaboration.

  1. The second misconception is that this meeting is not a status-update meeting either. It is used neither to report progress to the SM nor to the PO. Updating status is not the purpose of the meeting; rather, the point is to give every team member a clear understanding of everyone else’s work, so as to support further collaboration during the day.

  2. There is another misconception, one that many people slip into without noticing: this meeting is not meant for solving problems either. It is simply a very brief synchronization meeting among team members. To keep the meeting efficient, avoid long discussions that dive into details. Reflecting the team’s current progress and identifying obstacles to the work is enough to achieve its purpose.

The Purpose of the Daily Standup

So, with these misconceptions cleared up, the purpose of the standup becomes fairly clear:

  1. The team itself owns the meeting. A very mature Scrum team may not even need the SM to organize and facilitate the standup.

  2. The main purpose of the meeting is to synchronize the team’s progress. Members learn about one another’s progress so that everyone knows where the team currently stands in terms of achieving the sprint goal, and what still needs to be adjusted.

  3. Finally, the standup also surfaces the main difficulties and impediments at present, making it easier to take timely action.

What Happens in the Standup

Because the standup’s main function is synchronization and collaboration, it is usually held at the start of the working day — the standup is the starting point of the team’s work for that day. The meeting typically follows a routine in which everyone gathers in front of the kanban board, and each team member takes turns answering three questions:

  • What did I accomplish yesterday?
  • What is my plan for today?
  • What difficulties have I run into, or what do I need others to collaborate with me on?

By answering these three questions, each member lets everyone else know their current progress, then works out whom they need to collaborate with that day and which issues need to be discussed as soon as possible. They state the support they need, or offer assistance when others need it.

Precisely because the standup’s function is to synchronize information, and because it is held every day, its duration should be strictly controlled and normally should not exceed 15 minutes. Everyone gives a quick update on their progress, and any issues requiring further discussion should be taken offline — discussed separately afterwards with the relevant people, going into the details or the solution in depth.

The Different Roles in the Standup

As for the three different roles in Scrum, what should each of them do when taking part in the standup, and what role should each play?

Scrum Master

As the team’s organizer and supporter, the SM’s main role in the standup is really to maintain the discipline of the standup, ensure the meeting runs efficiently, and keep it aligned with the Agile spirit.

  • When an issue arises that may need in-depth discussion, interrupt in time and move the issue into the parking lot section of the board, arranging to continue the discussion after the standup.

  • Based on the progress and work reported by team members, judge the risk to achieving the sprint goal, remind the team of any progress that may be falling behind, and coordinate other members to join in collaboration as appropriate.

  • If an impediment raised by a member cannot be resolved immediately within the team during the meeting, record it and follow up on its progress that same day.

  • Before the meeting ends, the SM can also quickly share the sprint’s current burndown chart and the status of the main items on the board with the team, so that everyone has an overall picture of the current progress.

  • Finally, the SM should keep the meeting within its time limit and end it in no more than 15 minutes.

A burndown chart is a fitted chart of the work actually completed against the ideal progress, and it intuitively shows whether the team’s current progress is on track.

Dev Team

  • Attend on time; do not be late.

  • Most important of all, of course, is synchronizing progress by clearly answering the three questions above.

  • Before the meeting, update the status of the tasks you own in time, so that the task status information on the board is accurate.

  • Any impediments, or issues that need coordination or clarification, should be raised promptly at the standup — this is, after all, the main purpose of the meeting.

PO

During the sprint, the PO’s main responsibility is to clarify and confirm requirements. But since the standup’s function is mainly to synchronize the team’s work progress, the PO is not necessarily required to attend. That said, attending is not off the table either — the PO’s participation has its value.

  • For the PO personally, taking part in the standup reveals the team’s current progress and allows a more timely and clearer judgment about whether the Sprint Goal will be met.

  • If there are questions about requirements or points needing clarification at the standup, ones that can be explained in a sentence or two can be resolved right in the meeting. For more complex ones, the PO can stay informed in time and follow up with a separate one-on-one conversation immediately afterwards.

  • Also, during the sprint, if requirements currently in progress are adjusted or their priorities change, this needs to be explained to the team at the standup in time, so the team can make the corresponding adjustments and responses.

  • Sometimes the difficulties or impediments the team identifies are related to the PO; in that case the PO can follow up promptly, including updating the team on the resolution progress of impediments that were reported earlier.

Overall, the requirements for the three roles in Scrum to attend the standup are:

  • SM - Not mandatory, but attendance is recommended.
  • Dev Team - All members must attend (including joining remotely by phone); if a member temporarily cannot attend, it is best to ask another member to speak on their behalf.
  • PO - Not required, but may attend.

Points to Note When Running It

Finally, whether the standup achieves its effect also depends on a number of points where many Agile teams’ practice tends to go off track. They are summarized below:

  • The meeting should be held at a fixed time and place. The standup runs every day, so everyone should form the habit of attending at the same fixed time and in the same fixed place each day, avoiding the time wasted on gathering people because of frequent changes.

  • Be brief. When speaking, every member should keep in mind that the meeting’s purpose is to synchronize progress, and simply explain the three related questions clearly. This is not the place to explore and solve problems. Keep each person’s speaking time to around one minute.

  • Be punctual. The standup requires all Dev Team members to take part, so that everyone clearly understands the others’ progress and can collaborate promptly on matters that need it. And because the standup is quite simple, attending on time matters all the more — no one should waste the team’s time for personal reasons.

When a member really is late, the meeting usually does not wait for everyone to arrive; the fixed start time must be strictly honored. (For team members working in different locations or remotely, they can dial in via video conference or phone, but attendance must still be ensured. If a team member goes on leave mid-sprint, they should normally entrust another member to report their progress on their behalf.)

  • Stay focused. This is a point that is easy to overlook. The reasoning is the same as above: because the standup’s function is collaboration, every member should stay focused on the meeting and make sure they clearly understand everyone’s progress. No one should be handling other work, taking phone calls, playing with their phone, or holding side conversations during the meeting.

  • Parking lot. This is a dedicated area on the board. When issues that need in-depth discussion inevitably come up at the standup, they are temporarily noted and placed in this separate area to keep the meeting efficient. The parking lot’s purpose is to prevent the meeting from slipping into deep discussion, while the relevant members can continue digging into those issues afterwards.

  • Stand-up meeting. As the name suggests, a standup is meant to be held with everyone standing. Especially for teams sharing one office, standing effectively keeps the meeting from dragging on too long; and for teams with a physical board, moving items on the board is more convenient while standing, while speaking while standing also makes it easier for everyone to hear clearly.

Summary

The standup is a routine information-synchronization ceremony during the sprint that every member attends. Efficiency therefore matters a great deal — it is an important expression of the team’s self-organization and effective collaboration. Grasping the standup’s purpose, along with the key points and considerations for each role’s participation, helps us run the standup better and truly carry forward the Agile spirit.

item.title: Scrum's Four Ceremonies: Sprint Planning
item.description:
In the Scrum agile model, the practical implementation of agility is actually accomplished mainly through the four main ceremonies defined by Scrum, that is, what we usually call the four agile ceremonies. In this article, we explore the role of the Sprint Planning meeting among the four ceremonies, as well as the key points of its practice.

The Role of the Planning Meeting

At the start of every Sprint, this Sprint Planning meeting is held first, and this meeting also marks the beginning of the Sprint.

The main role of this meeting, as its name suggests, is to formulate the plan for the current Sprint’s operation, to determine the team’s work content and work direction in the current Sprint, and to form the Sprint backlog, SBI.

Inputs to the Meeting

PBI

The most important input to the Planning meeting is the Product Backlog, PBI.

The main discussion in the meeting actually revolves mainly around the PBI, that is, extracting the backlog items jointly confirmed by the team from the PBI, bringing them into the current iteration, and forming the SBI

And the PBI used as an input to the meeting should be requirements that have already been refined and distilled together with the team. Team members should also have a full understanding of the requirements themselves and have completed estimates of the workload for the backlog items. All backlog items should also have defined priorities.

This is also the main reason why, before the Planning meeting is held, the PBI should preferably have already gone through requirement clarification and estimation in a grooming meeting, so as to improve the efficiency of the Planning meeting. Of course, during the Planning meeting there will also be further clarification and confirmation of requirements, but just to keep time under control, this part should be given as solid a foundation as possible in advance.

DOR/DOD

Another important input is the team’s collective definition of DOR and DOD, which is usually confirmed in Sprint 0. Subsequent Sprints can reuse it, and if there are revisions it is confirmed again.

Regarding DOR and DOD, we already explained them when introducing Sprint artifacts, so we will not go into detail again.

DOR is in fact the standard for pending requirements that can enter a Sprint; only requirements that meet DOR should enter the Planning discussion. DOD, on the other hand, is the standard by which each backlog item can be considered complete during the Sprint.

The Planning meeting should confirm that everyone has a shared understanding of this.

Capacity

This reflects the team’s production capacity. The capacity of team members in each Sprint is not fixed, because there may be members on leave, temporarily reassigned, or not fully dedicated to the project in the first place. Therefore, before the Planning meeting is held, the Scrum Master should gather and understand the overall Capacity of the team for the current Sprint in advance.

The Questions the Meeting Needs to Answer

In the Planning meeting, there are actually mainly three questions to answer: Why? What? How?

  • Why?

Why are we running this Sprint? The team needs to understand what value the work in this Sprint brings to the product. The PO needs to explain to everyone the value goal he hopes to achieve and be able to answer the team’s questions: why are we doing these requirements? Why should these requirements be placed in the current Sprint?

  • What? What exactly is to be done in the Sprint? If the requirements have already been refined and distilled through grooming, a lot of time will be saved here. But if the requirements have not been fully clarified, or if some new ideas arise during the meeting, the PO and the team need to work through the requirement details here, identify the relevant risks and dependencies, and reach a shared understanding.

  • How? This part is more a discussion for the development team members, namely determining exactly how the requirements brought into the Sprint will be implemented, and further breaking the requirement Stories down into different work tasks and matching them to people. The Scrum Master will work with the team to complete task assignment and balance the team’s Capacity.

Outputs of the Meeting

The most important output of the Planning meeting is, of course, the SBI, which contains all the task items that need to be completed in the current iteration.

In addition, there is another artifact we introduced earlier, the Sprint Goal. This sets out a summary of the goal that the team and the PO have jointly agreed the iteration should strive to accomplish.

Meeting Duration

Empirical data from agile organizations is 2 hours per week based on the length of the Sprint; that is, if the Sprint is 1 week, the Sprint planning meeting takes about 2 hours, while a Sprint is usually 2 weeks long, in which case the Sprint planning meeting takes 4 hours.

Of course this is only empirical data, and it will vary for different teams depending on team size, maturity, and the complexity of the work.

How Different Roles Should Participate

The Planning meeting is mainly an internal team meeting, and its participants include all team members. In a small number of cases, key stakeholders (the direct boss) may be invited; when they are needed to provide some decision-making input, they may be invited to attend. For relatively large projects where multiple Scrum teams collaborate, key engineers from other teams may also be invited to participate in some important technical assessments. But on the whole, this meeting is still mainly an internal team discussion, with participants being the PO, SM, and Dev Team.

PO

Before the planning meeting, the PO needs to complete the prioritization of the PBI and finish the grooming of requirements with the team in advance.

During the meeting, the PO mainly needs to answer the Why and What questions, propose the expected Sprint Goal, and confirm the Scope.

At the end of the meeting, the PO should confirm the meeting outputs together with the team: the Sprint Goal and the SBI.

SM

Before the meeting, the Scrum Master needs to schedule the meeting and gather the team’s committed capacity, which people need to take leave, and the time each member will invest in the Sprint.

During the meeting, the SM is responsible for facilitating, organizing the meeting process, assisting the team with task breakdown and work assignment, and ensuring that all tasks in the Scope have a corresponding owner.

During task assignment and claiming, the SM should constantly check the match between team members’ tasks and their available personal time to avoid over-commitment. This also includes coordinating on some mutually dependent tasks.

Finally, the SM is responsible for compiling the SBI and confirming the goal together with the team. There is usually also a step of collecting everyone’s confidence index about completing the Sprint goal.

After the meeting, the SM should also prepare the Sprint board, set the relevant tasks to their initial state, and send out the meeting minutes.

Dev Team

Before the meeting, team members should inform the SM of the time they will personally invest in the current iteration, participate in the PO’s grooming in advance, and fully understand the relevant requirement details in the PBI.

During the meeting, they should make sure they understand the Sprint’s goal; in addition, if any requirement needs further explanation, they should actively participate in refinement, understand the requirement, complete estimation, and proactively raise and discuss the identified risks and dependencies. Then, together with the team, they claim tasks according to their Capacity in the iteration and commit to the output).

Finally, everyone jointly confirms the Sprint goal and gives their own confidence index about the Sprint completing the goal, completing the launch of the Sprint

Meeting Process

Let us once again outline the overall process of how the meeting is conducted

After the SM convenes the meeting,

  1. The PO first explains the expected Sprint goal and the work scope of the current Sprint, and gives the relevant reasons and an explanation of the value to the product. The team discusses this part together and preliminarily determines the scope and goal

  2. Next, the requirements in the Scope are clarified one by one against DOR. For requirements that have not been groomed, refinement, clarification, and workload estimation are completed at this point. At the same time, possible risks and dependencies are identified and response measures are discussed.

These two stages are the first half of the Planning meeting, and also the PO’s home ground

  1. The second half that follows is the development team’s home ground. For the requirements already understood, tasks are further broken down and specifically assigned to people. Based on task claiming, the SM should simultaneously observe how Capacity matches up, ensuring there are no omitted tasks and no over-commitment. In this stage, depending on the situation, the PO is not required to attend; even if attending, it is mainly to answer questions about requirements that come up in the discussion.

  2. Finally, all team members jointly confirm the agreed Sprint goal and produce the SBI. This also represents the team’s commitment to the goal and scope. Finally, the whole team can give a confidence index (0~5) for successfully completing the Sprint.

Throughout the meeting, the SM is responsible for facilitating, and should control the meeting pace and pay attention to progress and time.

Summary

From the explanation above, you should be able to see that the Sprint planning meeting is a very critical meeting in agile operations:

  • Through the planning meeting, a clear Sprint goal is produced

  • Before the team officially starts the Sprint, the planning meeting enables full communication, making the overall work scope and goals transparent to all members and enhancing understanding

  • It matches the team’s capacity with the work tasks brought into the iteration as accurately as possible

  • Through breakdown and claiming, every backlog requirement has a clear owner

  • The team collectively completes the SBI and the goal, strengthening mutual cooperation and also laying the confidence for completing the iteration
